source_text: Παρέῤῥιψε δ᾿ ὁ Κέλσος καὶ τό· θεὸν δὲ καὶ θεοῦ υἱὸν οὐδεὶς ἐκ τοιούτων συμβόλων καὶ παρακουσμάτων οὐδ᾿ ἐξ οὕτως ἀγεννῶν τεκμηρίων συνίστησιν. ἐχρῆν δὲ αὐτὸν τὰ παρακούσματα ἐκθέμενον ἐλέγξαι καὶ τὰ ἀγεννῆ τεκμήρια λόγῳ παραστῆσαι· ἵν᾿ εἴ τι πιθανὸν ἐδόκει λέγειν ὁ Χριστιανὸς. ἀγωνίσασθαι πρὸς αὐτὸ πειραθῇ καὶ ἀνατρέψαι τὸν λόγον. ὅπερ δὲ εἶπε περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἀπήντησε μὲν ὡς περὶ μεγάλου, οὐκ ἐβουλήθη δὲ ἰδεῖν ὅτι τοῦτ᾿ ἀπήντησεν. ὡς ἡ ἐνάργεια παρίστησι περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ. ὡς γὰρ ὁ ἥλιος, φησὶ. πάντα τὰ ἄλλα φωτίζων πρῶτον αὑτὸν δεικνύει. οὕτως ἐχρῆν πεποιηκέναι τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ. εἴποιμεν ἂν οὖν ὅτι καὶ πεποίηκεν· „ἀνέτειλε“ γὰρ „ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις αὐτοῦ δικαιοσύνη, καὶ πλῆθος εἰρήνης“ γέγονεν ἀρξάμενον ἀπὸ τῆς γενέσεως αὐτοῦ, εὐτρεπίζοντος τοῦ θεοῦ τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ αὐτοῦ τὰ ἔθνη, ἵν᾿ ὑπὸ ἕνα γένηται τῶν Ῥωμαίων βασιλέα, καὶ μὴ διὰ τὸ προφάσει τῶν πολλῶν βασιλειῶν ἄμικτον τῶν ἐθνῶν πρὸς ἄλληλα χαλεπώτερον γένηται τοῖς ἀποστόλοις τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τὸ ποιῆσαι ὅπερ προσέταξεν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἰπών· „πορευθέντες μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη.“ καὶ σαφές γε ὅτι κατὰ τὴν Αὐγούστου βασιλείαν ὁ Ἰησοῦς γεγέννηται, τοῦ. ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, ὁμαλίσαντος διὰ μιᾶς βασιλείας τοὺς πολλοὺς τῶν ἐπὶ γῆς. ἦν δ᾿ ἂν ἐμπόδιον τοῦ νεμηθῆναι τὴν Ἰησοῦ διδασκαλίαν εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην τὸ πολλὰς εἶναι βασιλείας οὐ μόνον διὰ τὰ προειρημένα ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ τὸ ἀναγκάζεσθαι στρατεύεσθαι καὶ ὑπὲρ τῶν πατρίδων πολεμεῖν τοὺς πανταχοῦ· ὅ τε ἐγίνετο πρὸ τῶν Αὐγούστου χρόνων καὶ ἔτι γε ἀνωτέρω, ὅτε γε χρεία ἦν ὡς Πελοποννσίων καὶ Ἀθηναίων εἶναι πόλεμον οὕτω καὶ ἑτέρων πρὸς ἑτέρους. πῶς οὖν οἷόν τε ἦν τὴν εἰρηνικὴν ταύτην διδασκαλίαν καὶ μηδὲ ἐχθροὺς ἐπιτρέπουσαν ἀμύνεσθαι κρατῆσαι, εἰ μὴ τὰ τῆς οἰκουμένης τῇ Ἰησοῦ ἐπιδημίᾳ μετεβέβλητο πανταχοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ ἡμερώτερον;
pass_a_gloss: Celsus also tossed in (παρέρριψε) this: 'No one establishes (συνίστησιν) God and Son of God from such tokens/signs (σύμβολα) and mishearings/misunderstandings (παρακούσματα), nor from such ignoble/base (ἀγεννῆ) evidences (τεκμήρια).' But he ought, having set out the misunderstandings, to refute (ἐλέγξαι) them and to show by reason (λόγῳ) the ignoble evidences, so that, if the Christian seemed to say something plausible, he might try to contend (ἀγωνίσασθαι) against it and overturn (ἀνατρέψαι) the argument. But what he said about Jesus did turn out/come to pass (ἀπήντησε) as about a great one, but he did not wish (ἐβουλήθη) to see that this turned out, as the plain evidence (ἐνάργεια) establishes about Jesus. For 'as the sun (ἥλιος),' he says, 'lighting (φωτίζων) all the other things, first shows (δεικνύει) itself, so the Son of God ought to have done.' We would say then that he has also done [so]: for 'there dawned (ἀνέτειλε) in his days righteousness (δικαιοσύνη), and abundance (πλῆθος) of peace (εἰρήνη)' has come about, having begun from his birth (γένεσις), God making ready (εὐτρεπίζοντος) the nations for his teaching, that they might come under one king (βασιλεύς) of the Romans, and that, through the unmixed state (ἄμικτον) of the nations toward one another on account of (προφάσει) the many kingdoms (βασιλεῖαι), it might not become harder for the apostles of Jesus to do what Jesus commanded them, saying: 'Going, make disciples of (μαθητεύσατε) all the nations.' And it is clear that Jesus was born in the reign of Augustus, who, so to name it, levelled (ὁμαλίσαντος) through one kingdom the many of those on earth. And there would have been a hindrance (ἐμπόδιον) to Jesus' teaching being distributed (νεμηθῆναι) into the whole inhabited world (οἰκουμένη) — the existence of many kingdoms — not only through the things said before but also through those everywhere being compelled to serve as soldiers (στρατεύεσθαι) and to wage war (πολεμεῖν) for their fatherlands (πατρίδες); which happened before the times of Augustus and still earlier, when there was need for there to be war, as of Peloponnesians and Athenians, so also of others against others. How then was it possible for this peaceful (εἰρηνική) teaching, which does not even permit (ἐπιτρέπουσαν) defending oneself against/avenging oneself on (ἀμύνεσθαι) enemies (ἐχθροί), to prevail (κρατῆσαι), unless the affairs of the inhabited world had been changed (μετεβέβλητο) everywhere by/at the coming (ἐπιδημία) of Jesus toward the gentler (ἡμερώτερον)?
pass_b_english: Celsus also threw in this remark: “No one proves anyone to be God and the Son of God from such signs and misunderstandings, nor from evidence so ignoble.” He ought to have set out the misunderstandings and refuted them, and shown by reasoning that the evidence is ignoble, so that, if the Christian seemed to say anything persuasive, he might try to contend against it and overturn the argument. But what he said about Jesus did come true, as of someone great, though he did not wish to see that it had come true, as the plain facts about Jesus make evident. “For as the sun,” he says, “lighting up all other things, first shows itself, so the Son of God ought to have done.”

We would say, then, that he has indeed done so. For “in his days righteousness dawned, and abundance of peace” (Psalm 72:7) came about, beginning from his birth. God was preparing the nations for his teaching, so that they would come under one Roman emperor, and so that the nations’ lack of contact with one another, owing to the many kingdoms, would not make it harder for Jesus’ apostles to do what Jesus commanded them when he said: “Go and make disciples of all the nations” (Matthew 28:19).

It is clear that Jesus was born in the reign of Augustus, who, if I may put it so, brought the many peoples of the earth to one level under a single kingdom. The existence of many kingdoms would have hindered the spread of Jesus’ teaching through the whole world, not only for the reasons already given, but also because people everywhere were forced to serve as soldiers and to fight for their homelands. That was what happened before the times of Augustus and still earlier, whenever there was need for a war, as between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians, and so too between other peoples. How, then, could this teaching of peace, which does not even allow people to avenge themselves on enemies (Matthew 5:38–44), have prevailed, unless at the coming of Jesus the affairs of the world had everywhere been changed to a gentler state?

choices.why: θεὸν ... συνίστησιν: 'No one establishes God and the Son of God' (reads as proving God exists) -> 'No one proves anyone to be God and the Son of God'; 'such ignoble evidence' -> 'evidence so ignoble' (οὕτως ἀγεννῶν)
sun simile: γάρ and φησί sit inside Celsus's sentence, so the attribution now reads '"For as the sun," he says, "..."' as the Greek frames it
καὶ πεποίηκεν: 'he has done so' -> 'he has indeed done so'
verified: Psalm 72:7 = LXX 71:7 (Origen's aorist ἀνέτειλε noted); Matthew 28:19; Matthew 5:38–44 as summary allusion for non-retaliation

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; English is from the Greek.

Independent clause review: every clause checked; verdict pass.
Scripture citations sit inline beside the clause in Pass B.
2.30: 'τοὺς πολλοὺς τῶν ἐπὶ γῆς' is kept as 'the many peoples of the earth'; it could also mean 'most of those on earth'

translator_notes: Celsus’s two remarks (the ‘signs and misunderstandings’ sentence, and the sun simile with ‘he says’) are direct statements in the Greek and are in double quotation marks. ‘God’ and ‘Son of God’ are capitalised in Celsus’s sentence because they name the Christian claim about Christ. ‘ὅπερ δὲ εἶπε... ἀπήντησε’ looks forward to the sun simile: what Celsus demanded has in fact happened. Psalm 72:7 = LXX Psalm 71:7, which reads the future ‘ἀνατελεῖ’ (will dawn); Origen quotes it as an aorist ‘ἀνέτειλε’ (dawned), rendered as Origen has it; δικαιοσύνη rendered ‘righteousness’ as in English versions of the verse. ‘ὑπὸ ἕνα... τῶν Ῥωμαίων βασιλέα’ rendered ‘under one Roman emperor’ (βασιλεύς is the usual Greek title for the emperor). ‘teaching... which does not even allow people to avenge themselves on enemies’ is an allusion to the Sermon on the Mount on non-retaliation and love of enemies, cited inline as Matthew 5:38–44 (summary allusion, not a quotation). The source misprints ‘Πελοποννσίων’ for ‘Πελοποννησίων’. ‘τῇ Ἰησοῦ ἐπιδημίᾳ’ may be temporal (at the coming) or instrumental (by the coming); rendered ‘at the coming’. Reviewer: in Celsus’s first remark the object of συνίστησιν is implicit; ‘proves anyone to be God and the Son of God’ supplies it, since ‘establishes God’ would wrongly suggest proving that God exists.
